docs.title: Rust Programming: From Zero to Useful
docs.text: Learn Rust from first principles to a small command-line application.

docs.title: Course target
docs.text: By the end, you will be able to write, test, and package small Rust programs with confidence.

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text:
This course is for programmers who are new to Rust. You should be comfortable with a terminal and basic programming ideas such as variables, functions, and conditionals. Install the stable Rust toolchain with rustup before starting.

Start with Module 0: First lesson, then use the roadmap and syllabus to plan the track.

docs.title: Final goal
docs.text:
Build a tested command-line task tracker while learning Rust's ownership model, types, error handling, and project tooling.

Milestone Modules Outcome Foundation 0–2 Compile Rust, use core types, and understand ownership. Application 3–4 Handle errors and organize code into a Cargo project. Capstone 5+ Build and test a useful command-line task tracker.

docs.title: Recommended sequence
docs.text:
1. Start with Module 0 and compile every example locally.
  2. Learn ownership before borrowing, collections, and error handling.
  3. Integrate each concept into the capstone only after the small example works.

docs.title: 0. Hello, Rust
docs.text:
• Install the toolchain and compile a first Rust program.
  • Read the shape of a main function and a println! macro.
  • Make a small change and observe the compiler feedback.

Add one section per module and link it to the module overview.

docs.title: Module 0: Set up Rust and build Hello World
By the end, you will be able to
docs.text:
• Install the stable Rust toolchain with rustup.
  • Explain the jobs of rustup, rustc, and Cargo.
  • Build, run, format, check, and package a small application.

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
Rust programs start at a function named main. The println! macro writes a line of text to the terminal. Rust checks the program before running it, so mistakes are reported early by the compiler.

flowchart LR
  A[main function] --> B[println! macro]
  B --> C[Compiled binary]

docs.title: Install the toolchain
docs.text:
The recommended installer is rustup. On Linux, macOS, or WSL, run:

curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh

Accept the default stable toolchain, then open a new terminal so the Cargo bin directory is on your PATH. On Windows, download and run rustup-init.exe from the official installation page. Windows builds may also need the Visual Studio C++ build tools.

Verify the installation:

rustup show
rustc --version
cargo --version

Keep the stable toolchain current with rustup update. If a command is not found after installation, restart the terminal and check that $HOME/.cargo/bin is on PATH.

docs.title: The important commands
docs.text:
Command Job rustup Installs and selects Rust toolchains and components. rustc Compiles a Rust source file directly. cargo Creates, builds, runs, tests, documents, and packages projects. rustfmt Formats Rust source consistently. clippy Finds common mistakes and non-idiomatic Rust. rustdoc Generates API documentation from Rust comments. rust-analyzer Gives editor features such as completion and diagnostics.

The standard stable installation includes Cargo, rustfmt, and Clippy. If a component is missing, install it explicitly:

rustup component add rustfmt clippy
rustup component add rust-src  # useful for rust-analyzer

Most editors install or bundle rust-analyzer; VS Code uses the official extension. The compiler tools work independently of any editor.

docs.title: Create a Hello World application
docs.text:
Cargo keeps the source layout and build metadata together. From the repository root, create a new application in a temporary directory:

cargo new /tmp/hello-rust
cd /tmp/hello-rust

Cargo creates Cargo.toml and src/main.rs. Replace src/main.rs with:

fn main() {
    println!("Hello, Rust!");
}

docs.title: Build, run, and package it
docs.text:
Run these commands inside /tmp/hello-rust:

cargo check                 # type-check quickly without creating a binary
cargo build                 # debug build in target/debug/
cargo run                   # build if needed, then run the binary
cargo run -- Rust           # pass Rust as an argument to the binary
cargo build --release       # optimized build in target/release/
cargo test                  # run tests, when the project has tests
cargo doc --open            # build and open local API documentation
cargo package --allow-dirty # validate the package archive locally

For this application, the release binary is target/release/hello-rust on Linux and macOS, or target/release/hello-rust.exe on Windows. cargo package creates a crate archive for distribution and checks that the package can be published. It does not upload anything. Use cargo publish only when you intend to publish a crate to crates.io.

docs.title: Format and lint before sharing
docs.text:
cargo fmt                 # format the whole project
cargo fmt -- --check      # fail if formatting would change files
cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings

rustfmt handles layout. Clippy provides advice about correctness, performance, and idiomatic style. Treat warnings as errors in CI when the project is ready for that policy.

The commands above are the standard Rust workflow: check, format, lint, test, build, then create a release artifact.

docs.title: Run the course example
docs.text:
The repository also contains a Cargo version of Hello World:

cargo run --manifest-path examples/00-first-lesson/hello-world/Cargo.toml

Expected output:

Hello, Rust!

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Change the message in examples/00-first-lesson/hello-world/src/main.rs, run cargo fmt, and use cargo run --manifest-path examples/00-first-lesson/hello-world/Cargo.toml to see the result.

docs.title: Review
docs.text:
1. Which command manages Rust toolchains?
  2. Which command runs the current Cargo package?
  3. Which command formats Rust source code?

docs.title: Cargo workspace with a binary and library
By the end, you will be able to
docs.text:
• Create a workspace containing an executable and a library package.
  • Split library code into two modules.
  • Import and call library functions from the executable.

docs.title: Workspace layout
docs.text:
A workspace groups related Cargo packages under one root manifest. In this example, app is the executable and toolkit is the library:

cargo-workspace/
├── Cargo.toml
├── app/
│   ├── Cargo.toml
│   └── src/main.rs
└── toolkit/
    ├── Cargo.toml
    └── src/
        ├── lib.rs
        ├── greetings.rs
        └── numbers.rs

The root Cargo.toml lists both packages:

[workspace]
members = ["app", "toolkit"]
resolver = "2"

The workspace root does not need its own src/ directory.

docs.title: The library package
docs.text:
toolkit/Cargo.toml identifies the library package:

[package]
name = "toolkit"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

Declare the two modules in toolkit/src/lib.rs and re-export their public functions:

pub mod greetings;
pub mod numbers;

The first module, toolkit/src/greetings.rs, contains a greeting function:

pub fn hello(name: &str) -> String {
    format!("Hello, {name}!")
}

The second module, toolkit/src/numbers.rs, contains a calculation:

pub fn add(left: i32, right: i32) -> i32 {
    left + right
}

pub makes the modules and functions available outside the library crate.

docs.title: The executable package
docs.text:
Declare the library as a path dependency in app/Cargo.toml:

[package]
name = "app"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

[dependencies]
toolkit = { path = "../toolkit" }

The executable imports both modules and calls one function from each:

use toolkit::{greetings, numbers};

fn main() {
    println!("{}", greetings::hello("workspace"));
    println!("2 + 3 = {}", numbers::add(2, 3));
}

Expected output:

Hello, workspace!
2 + 3 = 5

The dependency graph is:

flowchart LR
  W[Workspace] --> A[app binary]
  A --> T[toolkit library]
  T --> G[greetings module]
  T --> N[numbers module]

docs.title: Build and run the workspace
docs.text:
Run these commands from the workspace root:

cargo check
cargo test
cargo run -p app
cargo build --release -p app

Cargo builds the library before linking the executable. The release executable is written to target/release/app on Linux.

You can also run the package by manifest path from the repository root:

cargo run --manifest-path examples/00-first-lesson/cargo-workspace/app/Cargo.toml

Cargo finds the workspace root by following the package's parent directories.

docs.title: Tests belong next to the code they verify
docs.text:
The demo puts unit tests in the library modules:

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::add;

    #[test]
    fn adds_two_numbers() {
        assert_eq!(add(2, 3), 5);
    }
}

Run all workspace tests with:

cargo test

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
How does the executable use the local library package?

By copying lib.rs into main.rs By publishing the library first By declaring a path dependency in app/Cargo.toml Check answer

docs.title: By the end, you will be able to
docs.text:
• Build a Rust release binary with Cargo.
  • Package it as a Debian .deb file.
  • Install and remove the package on Debian or Ubuntu.

docs.title: The workflow
docs.text:
cargo-deb reads your Cargo project, builds the release binary, and places it inside a Debian package with metadata from Cargo.toml.

flowchart LR
  S[Rust source] --> C[Cargo build]
  C --> P[cargo-deb]
  P --> D[.deb package]
  D --> I[apt install]

This lesson assumes a binary Cargo project with a Cargo.toml file and a src/main.rs entry point.

docs.title: 1. Prepare the project
docs.text:
From the project root, check, format, lint, and test before packaging:

cargo fmt -- --check
cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings
cargo test
cargo build --release

The release binary is written to target/release/<binary-name>.

docs.title: 2. Install the Debian packager
docs.text:
Install the Cargo subcommand once:

cargo install cargo-deb

If installation reports that Rust is too old, update the Rust toolchain first:

rustup update

docs.title: 3. Add package metadata
docs.text:
A basic binary can be packaged without extra configuration. Add metadata when you want a maintainer, section, or explicit runtime dependencies:

[package.metadata.deb]
maintainer = "Your Name <you@example.com>"
section = "utils"
priority = "optional"
depends = "$auto"

The package name and version come from the [package] section:

[package]
name = "hello-rust"
version = "0.1.0"

docs.title: 4. Create the .deb file
docs.text:
Run this from the directory containing Cargo.toml:

cargo deb

The result is written to target/debian/. Its filename contains the package name, version, Debian revision, and architecture, for example:

target/debian/hello-rust_0.1.0-1_amd64.deb

To package the course Hello World project from the repository root:

cargo deb \
  --manifest-path examples/00-first-lesson/hello-world/Cargo.toml

docs.title: 5. Inspect and install it
docs.text:
Inspect the archive before installing it:

dpkg-deb --info target/debian/hello-rust_*.deb
dpkg-deb --contents target/debian/hello-rust_*.deb

Install it locally with apt, which can resolve package dependencies:

sudo apt install ./target/debian/hello-rust_*.deb

Run the installed program:

hello-rust

Remove it later with:

sudo apt remove hello-rust

docs.title: Architecture matters
docs.text:
A .deb is built for a target architecture. Check the architecture of the current machine with:

dpkg --print-architecture

For a specific Rust target, install the target toolchain and pass it to cargo-deb:

rustup target add x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
cargo deb --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu

Cross-compilation may also require a linker and system libraries for the target architecture.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
Which command creates the Debian package?

cargo publish cargo deb rustc --deb Check answer

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The repeatable release path is:

cargo fmt -- --check
cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings
cargo test
cargo deb
sudo apt install ./target/debian/*.deb

docs.title: By the end, you will be able to
docs.text:
• Find the important files produced by Cargo on Linux.
  • Tell debug output from release output.
  • Inspect a Rust executable with standard Linux tools.

docs.title: A small demo project
docs.text:
The demo contains one binary and one library target:

linux-compiler-output/
├── Cargo.toml
└── src/
    ├── lib.rs
    └── main.rs

Cargo discovers src/main.rs as the executable target and src/lib.rs as the library target.

Build it from the repository root:

cargo build --manifest-path examples/00-first-lesson/linux-compiler-output/Cargo.toml
cargo build --manifest-path examples/00-first-lesson/linux-compiler-output/Cargo.toml --release

Run it:

cargo run --manifest-path examples/00-first-lesson/linux-compiler-output/Cargo.toml

Expected output:

Hello from a Linux Rust binary
2 + 3 = 5

docs.title: What Cargo creates
docs.text:
Cargo puts compiler output in target/ by default. The profile directory separates normal development builds from optimized release builds:

Path Meaning target/debug/ Development build with fast compilation and debug information. target/release/ Optimized build intended for distribution. target/debug/<name> Debug executable. target/release/<name> Release executable. target/debug/deps/ Dependency and intermediate artifacts. target/debug/incremental/ Incremental compiler cache. target/doc/ Output from cargo doc. target/package/ Output from cargo package.

The exact contents of deps/, incremental/, and build-script directories are compiler internals. Do not copy them to a target machine.

docs.title: Common file types
docs.text:
File Meaning No extension on Linux Usually an executable binary. .rlib Rust library artifact used by the Rust compiler. .rmeta Rust metadata used during compilation. .so Dynamic shared library on Linux. .d Dependency information used to know when to rebuild. .o Object file used before final linking.

For normal application deployment, copy only the release executable or the final library package. The .rlib, .rmeta, .d, and .o files are not application deliverables.

docs.title: check versus build
docs.text:
cargo check --manifest-path examples/00-first-lesson/linux-compiler-output/Cargo.toml
cargo build --manifest-path examples/00-first-lesson/linux-compiler-output/Cargo.toml

cargo check runs the compiler's analysis without producing a final linked executable. It is fast and useful while editing. cargo build continues to link the final binary into target/debug/.

docs.title: Inspect the Linux executable
docs.text:
Use find to locate final binaries:

find examples/00-first-lesson/linux-compiler-output/target \
  -maxdepth 3 -type f -executable -print

Use file to identify the binary format and architecture:

file examples/00-first-lesson/linux-compiler-output/target/release/linux-compiler-output

On a typical 64-bit Linux host, the output includes ELF 64-bit and the machine architecture.

Use ldd to view dynamically linked system libraries:

ldd examples/00-first-lesson/linux-compiler-output/target/release/linux-compiler-output

Use readelf to inspect the ELF header without executing the program:

readelf -h examples/00-first-lesson/linux-compiler-output/target/release/linux-compiler-output

These commands inspect the final executable. They do not replace cargo build and should not be used to edit compiler output.

docs.title: The compiler pipeline
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  A[src/main.rs] --> B[rustc analysis]
  B --> C[object files and metadata]
  C --> D[Linux linker]
  D --> E[target/release/binary]

Cargo coordinates the process, rustc compiles Rust code, and the Linux linker combines object files and libraries into the final ELF executable.

docs.title: Clean and rebuild
docs.text:
cargo clean --manifest-path examples/00-first-lesson/linux-compiler-output/Cargo.toml
cargo build --manifest-path examples/00-first-lesson/linux-compiler-output/Cargo.toml --release

cargo clean removes generated build artifacts. It does not remove source files or Cargo.toml.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
Where does cargo build --release place the final binary?

target/debug/ target/release/ src/release/ Check answer

docs.title: Cross-compile Rust for a Raspberry Pi Pico
By the end, you will be able to
docs.text:
• Build Rust firmware for the RP2040 Cortex-M0+ processor.
  • Send Hello, Pico! to a computer over USB serial.
  • Flash the firmware through the Pico USB bootloader.
  • Understand how a debug probe enables breakpoints and stepping.

docs.title: What changes on a Pico?
docs.text:
A Linux Rust program targets the host operating system. Pico firmware is bare-metal code, so it needs a different target, a board memory layout, a startup runtime, and a flashing method.

The RP2040 uses two Cortex-M0+ cores. Rust targets it with thumbv6m-none-eabi.

flowchart LR
  A[Rust source] --> B[rustc for thumbv6m-none-eabi]
  B --> C[ARM ELF firmware]
  C --> D[UF2 or SWD flash]
  D --> E[RP2040 Pico]
  E --> F[USB CDC serial output]

The rp-pico board-support package configures the Pico pins and RP2040 HAL. The usb-device and usbd-serial crates expose a USB CDC-ACM serial port.

docs.title: Install the embedded toolchain
docs.text:
rustup target add thumbv6m-none-eabi
cargo install --locked elf2uf2-rs

elf2uf2-rs converts the ARM ELF output to UF2 and can copy it to the mounted RPI-RP2 bootloader drive. The demo uses rust-lld, so a separate ARM GCC compiler is not required.

docs.title: Project configuration
docs.text:
The demo's .cargo/config.toml selects the cross target and linker script:

[build]
target = "thumbv6m-none-eabi"

[target.thumbv6m-none-eabi]
linker = "rust-lld"
runner = "elf2uf2-rs -d"
rustflags = [
    "-C", "link-arg=--nmagic",
    "-C", "link-arg=-Tlink.x",
]

memory.x describes the Pico's flash and RAM layout. Keeping it beside Cargo.toml lets the linker use the board's memory map directly.

docs.title: USB Hello Pico application
docs.text:
The application is #![no_std] and #![no_main]. It initializes the RP2040 clocks, creates a USB CDC serial class, and writes a greeting while polling USB.

// A bare-metal firmware has no operating system or standard library.
#![no_std]
// The Cortex-M runtime supplies the entry point instead of a normal `main` ABI.
#![no_main]

// Halt the processor if an unrecoverable panic occurs.
use panic_halt as _;
// `entry` marks the reset entry point, `hal` provides board drivers, and `pac`
// exposes the RP2040 peripheral registers.
use rp_pico::{entry, hal, pac};
// USB device traits and the CDC serial class used by the host terminal.
use usb_device::{class_prelude::*, prelude::*};
use usbd_serial::SerialPort;

// Firmware entry points never return, so the function returns the never type.
#[entry]
fn main() -> ! {
    // Take ownership of the device peripherals exactly once after reset.
    let mut peripherals = pac::Peripherals::take().unwrap();
    // The watchdog is required while the RP2040 clocks are configured.
    let mut watchdog = hal::Watchdog::new(peripherals.WATCHDOG);

    // Configure the Pico oscillator, system PLL, and USB PLL.
    let clocks = hal::clocks::init_clocks_and_plls(
        rp_pico::XOSC_CRYSTAL_FREQ,
        peripherals.XOSC,
        peripherals.CLOCKS,
        peripherals.PLL_SYS,
        peripherals.PLL_USB,
        &mut peripherals.RESETS,
        &mut watchdog,
    )
    .ok()
    .unwrap();

    // Create the USB bus that owns the RP2040 USB peripheral and its DPRAM.
    let usb_bus = UsbBusAllocator::new(hal::usb::UsbBus::new(
        peripherals.USBCTRL_REGS,
        peripherals.USBCTRL_DPRAM,
        clocks.usb_clock,
        true,
        &mut peripherals.RESETS,
    ));

    // Add a USB CDC-ACM serial interface to the bus.
    let mut serial = SerialPort::new(&usb_bus);
    // Describe the USB device to the host computer.
    let mut usb_device = UsbDeviceBuilder::new(&usb_bus, UsbVidPid(0x16c0, 0x27dd))
        .strings(&[StringDescriptors::default().product("Hello Pico")])
        .unwrap()
        .build();

    loop {
        // Poll services USB enumeration and transfer events.
        if usb_device.poll(&mut [&mut serial]) {
            // The demo ignores WouldBlock to keep the example small.
            let _ = serial.write(b"Hello from Pico!\r\n");
        }
    }
}

The same code is in the demo's src/main.rs.

docs.title: What happens at startup?
docs.text:
1. #![no_std] removes the operating-system-dependent Rust standard library.
  2. #[entry] tells cortex-m-rt which function runs after reset.
  3. pac::Peripherals::take() gives the firmware unique access to hardware registers.
  4. The watchdog and PLL setup produce the system and USB clocks.
  5. UsbBus owns the RP2040 USB peripheral and its packet memory.
  6. SerialPort creates a USB CDC-ACM interface that Linux exposes as a serial device such as /dev/ttyACM0.
  7. poll keeps USB enumeration and transfers moving. When it reports an event, the example writes Hello from Pico! to the serial endpoint.

The current demo writes on every successful poll event, so a terminal may show the greeting repeatedly while USB traffic is active. That is intentional for a small polling demonstration. A production logger would handle WouldBlock, buffer messages, and usually rate-limit output.

docs.title: Project structure
docs.text:
rp2040-hello-pico/
├── .cargo/
│   └── config.toml
├── src/
│   └── main.rs
├── Cargo.toml
├── Cargo.lock
├── memory.x
├── .gitignore
└── target/
File or directory Role Cargo.toml Names the firmware package and declares Rust dependencies. Cargo.lock Records the exact dependency versions used for a reproducible build. .cargo/config.toml Selects thumbv6m-none-eabi, linker flags, and the flash runner. src/main.rs Contains the no_std firmware entry point and USB serial loop. memory.x Defines the RP2040 flash, boot2, and RAM addresses for the linker. .gitignore Keeps generated target/ files out of version control. target/ Generated compiler output. It is not source code and should not be committed.

The package is named pico_hellp to match the working demo. The rp-pico dependency supplies the board support package, usb-device supplies the USB device framework, usbd-serial supplies the CDC serial class, and panic-halt stops the CPU if an unrecoverable panic occurs.

docs.title: Build the firmware
docs.text:
From the repository root, enter the demo directory first so Cargo discovers the embedded .cargo/config.toml:

cd examples/00-first-lesson/rp2040-hello-pico
cargo check
cargo build --release

The final ELF is written under:

target/thumbv6m-none-eabi/release/pico_hellp

docs.title: Flash over USB bootloader
docs.text:
1. Hold the Pico's BOOTSEL button.
  2. Connect the Pico to USB.
  3. Release BOOTSEL after the RPI-RP2 drive appears.
  4. Run:
cargo run --release

The configured elf2uf2-rs -d runner converts and copies the firmware. You can also create a UF2 file without flashing it:

elf2uf2-rs target/thumbv6m-none-eabi/release/pico_hellp hello-pico.uf2

Copy hello-pico.uf2 to the mounted RPI-RP2 drive, then wait for the Pico to reboot.

docs.title: Read the USB output
docs.text:
After the firmware boots, a new USB serial device should appear. On Linux it is often /dev/ttyACM0:

ls /dev/ttyACM*
screen /dev/ttyACM0 115200

The USB CDC connection does not use a physical baud rate, so 115200 is only a conventional terminal setting. Press Ctrl-A, then K to exit screen.

docs.title: Debugging the Pico
docs.text:
Yes, but USB serial output is logging, not source-level debugging. For breakpoints, stepping, register inspection, and memory inspection, use SWD with a debug probe such as a Raspberry Pi Debug Probe, J-Link, or a second Pico flashed with CMSIS-DAP debug-probe firmware.

Connect SWCLK, SWDIO, and GND from the probe to the target Pico. Install probe-rs and list the probe:

cargo install --locked probe-rs-tools
probe-rs list

Temporarily change the runner to:

runner = "probe-rs run --chip RP2040"

Then flash and run through SWD:

cargo run

The probe-rs VS Code extension can provide breakpoints and stepping. Keep debug information enabled in the debug profile so source lines map correctly.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
Which Rust target is used for an RP2040 Pico?

x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu thumbv6m-none-eabi wasm32-unknown-unknown Check answer

docs.title: Module 2: Ownership and borrowing
docs.text: This module moves from the basic ownership rule to advanced lifetime and API design patterns. Learn the topics in order because each stage depends on the mental model built by the previous one.

docs.title: 1. Values, variables, and scope
docs.text:
• Stack values versus heap-backed values
  • Scope and when a value is dropped
  • The difference between a value and the variable that owns it
  • Why String, Vec<T>, and other heap-backed types matter

Study Values, variables, and scope first.

docs.title: 2. Move semantics
docs.text:
• Assignment moves ownership for non-Copy types
  • Why using a moved value is a compile-time error
  • Passing ownership into a function
  • Returning ownership from a function
  • Reading compiler errors as ownership feedback

Continue with Move semantics.

docs.title: 3. Copy and Clone
docs.text:
• Which simple types implement Copy
  • Why Copy is different from an explicit clone()
  • The cost and intent of cloning heap-backed data
  • Designing types that should or should not be copied

docs.title: 4. Shared borrowing
docs.text:
• References with &T
  • Passing a reference without transferring ownership
  • Multiple shared references at the same time
  • Reference scope and the last use of a reference
  • Slices such as &str and &[T]

Start with Ownership and shared borrowing.

docs.title: 5. Mutable borrowing
docs.text:
• Mutable references with &mut T
  • The one-mutable-reference rule
  • Why mutable and shared references cannot overlap
  • Reborrowing and short mutable-borrow scopes
  • Designing functions that mutate through references

docs.title: 6. Borrowing collections and iterators
docs.text:
• Borrowing elements from String, Vec<T>, and maps
  • Iterating with iter, iter_mut, and into_iter
  • Avoiding mutation while an element is borrowed
  • Returning references into collections safely

docs.title: 7. Slices and API boundaries
docs.text:
• Prefer &str over &String in read-only APIs
  • Prefer slices such as &[T] over concrete collections where possible
  • Choosing owned values versus borrowed parameters
  • Using AsRef, Borrow, and generic bounds when they add real value

docs.title: 8. Lifetimes: describing relationships
docs.text:
• Why a reference needs a valid lifetime
  • Lifetime annotations describe relationships, not durations
  • Shared lifetime parameters in functions
  • Returning a reference tied to an input
  • Why lifetimes do not make data live longer

docs.title: 9. Structs that contain references
docs.text:
• Lifetime parameters on structs and enums
  • Borrowed views versus owned data
  • 'static references and what they really mean
  • When a lifetime makes an API harder to use
  • Replacing a borrowed struct with an owned type when appropriate

docs.title: 10. Lifetime elision and method receivers
docs.text:
• The compiler's lifetime elision rules
  • Why common functions need no explicit annotations
  • Lifetimes in methods with &self and &mut self
  • When explicit annotations improve clarity

docs.title: 11. Ownership in enums and error handling
docs.text:
• Moving values into and out of Option<T> and Result<T, E>
  • Borrowing with as_ref and as_mut
  • Matching without moving unnecessarily

docs.title: Recommended checkpoints
docs.text:
At each stage, be able to answer these questions:

  1. Who owns this value right now?
  2. Is this operation moving, copying, cloning, or borrowing it?
  3. Can this reference outlive the value it points to?
  4. Would an owned value make this API simpler?

The goal is not to add lifetime annotations everywhere. The goal is to make ownership explicit enough that the compiler and the API communicate the same design.

docs.title: By the end, you will be able to
docs.text:
• Distinguish a value from the variable that owns it.
  • Explain the difference between stack and heap storage at a high level.
  • Predict when a variable leaves scope and its value is dropped.

docs.title: Values and variables
docs.text:
A value is data such as 42 or the text stored in a String. A variable is a name that lets the program use a value:

let score = 42;

Here, 42 is the value and score is the variable that owns it. By default, variables are immutable, so use let mut when the binding itself must change:

let mut score = 42;
score = 43;

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Scope is the part of the program where a variable is valid. A variable starts when its let statement runs and ends at the closing brace of its block.

fn main() {
    let outside = "available here";

    {
        let inside = "available only in this block";
        println!("{outside}, {inside}");
    }

    println!("{outside}");
    // println!("{inside}"); // would fail: `inside` is out of scope
}

Rust drops a value when its owner leaves scope. For a small stack value, this usually means the storage is no longer needed. For a heap-backed value such as String or Vec<T>, Rust also releases the heap allocation automatically.

flowchart TD
  A[Enter block] --> B[Create owner and value]
  B --> C[Use value]
  C --> D[Leave block]
  D --> E[Drop value]
  E --> F[Release owned resources]

docs.title: Stack and heap, briefly
docs.text:
The stack is fast storage for values with a known, simple layout, such as integers. The heap stores data whose size can change or whose ownership must outlive a single expression. A String value keeps a small handle on the stack and its text in a heap allocation.

The important ownership lesson is that the variable still owns the complete String, including the heap data. When the variable leaves scope, Rust cleans up the allocation without a manual free call.

The same rule applies to Vec<T>. A vector stores its elements in a heap allocation, while the Vec handle on the stack tracks the allocation. The variable owns both the handle and the elements it contains:

{
    let mut numbers = vec![1, 2, 3];
    numbers.push(4);
    println!("numbers: {numbers:?}");
} // numbers and its heap allocation are dropped here

Expected output:

numbers: [1, 2, 3, 4]

The vector is automatically cleaned up when the block ends. No manual deallocation is needed.

docs.title: Why heap-backed types matter
docs.text:
Real programs often need data whose size is known only while the program is running: user input, a file, a network response, or a collection of records. String, Vec<T>, and similar types keep that changing data on the heap while their small ownership handle stays on the stack.

That extra allocation is useful because the data can grow, but it also creates resources that must have one clear owner. Rust's ownership rules make sure the allocation is released exactly once and cannot be used after its owner has gone away. Borrowing then lets another function temporarily read or modify the data without taking ownership:

fn add_label(labels: &mut Vec<String>) {
    labels.push(String::from("Rust"));
}

fn main() {
    let mut labels = vec![String::from("safe")];
    add_label(&mut labels); // borrowed temporarily, then returned to `labels`
    println!("{labels:?}");
} // `labels` owns the vector and its strings until cleanup

Expected output:

["safe", "Rust"]

This is why heap-backed types are central to ownership and borrowing: they let Rust support flexible, useful data structures without requiring manual free, while still making the lifetime and access rules explicit.

docs.title: Complete runnable example
docs.text:
The lesson displays the same source file that you can compile from the matching examples/ directory. Keeping one source file prevents the lesson and demo from drifting apart.

fn main() {
    let score = 42;
    let message = String::from("Rust owns its data");

    println!("score: {score}");
    println!("message: {message}");

    {
        let temporary = String::from("temporary value");
        println!("inside: {temporary}");
    }

    println!("outside: still in scope");
}

docs.title: Memory after each step
docs.text: The diagrams below are conceptual. They explain ownership and lifetime, not literal addresses, stack offsets, allocator metadata, or an exact compiler layout.

docs.title: Step 1: create score
docs.text:
let score = 42;
Area State Stack score owns the integer value 42. Heap No allocation is needed for this integer. Scope score is valid until the end of main.

docs.title: Step 2: create message
docs.text:
let message = String::from("Rust owns its data");
Area State Stack message owns a String handle containing a pointer, length, and capacity. Heap The string characters are stored in an allocation owned by message. Scope message is valid until the end of main.

docs.title: Step 3: enter the inner scope
docs.text:
{
    let temporary = String::from("temporary value");
}
Area State Stack score, message, and temporary are valid in the inner block. Heap There are separate allocations for message and temporary. Scope temporary is valid only inside the inner block.

docs.title: Step 4: leave the inner scope
docs.text:
When the closing brace runs, temporary leaves scope first:

Area State Stack The temporary binding is gone. score and message remain. Heap The allocation owned by temporary is released. message remains allocated. Scope Code after the block can still use score and message.

docs.title: Step 5: leave main
docs.text:
At the end of main, Rust drops the remaining owners automatically:

Area State Stack score and the message handle leave scope. Heap The allocation owned by message is released. Result No manual free call is needed.

docs.title: By the end, you will be able to
docs.text:
• Predict when assigning a heap-backed value moves ownership.
  • Explain why the old variable cannot be used after a move.
  • Recognize ownership transfer into and out of functions.
  • Read a moved-value compiler error as useful design feedback.

docs.title: The intuition: one owner, one cleanup
docs.text:
For a heap-backed value such as String, the variable contains a small handle that points to data on the heap. If Rust copied that handle during assignment, two variables could try to release the same allocation. Rust avoids that problem by moving ownership: the destination becomes the owner and the source binding is no longer usable.

let first = String::from("hello");
let second = first; // ownership moves from `first` to `second`
println!("{second}");

The text is not copied by this assignment. The String handle and its heap allocation now belong to second. The compiler rejects this because first is no longer an owner:

// println!("{first}");

This is a compile-time rule, so the program cannot accidentally use a moved value or free its allocation twice.

The diagram is conceptual: it shows ownership and pointers, not literal addresses or the exact allocator representation.

docs.title: Compiler errors are ownership feedback
docs.text:
When the compiler reports borrow of moved value, read it as a short ownership history. It means:

  1. A value had an owner.
  2. An operation moved ownership somewhere else.
  3. Later code tried to use the old binding.

Here is a deliberately tricky example. The println! looks harmless because it only reads title, but reading still requires the binding to be valid:

fn main() {
    let title = String::from("Rust ownership");
    let archived_title = title; // The String moves to `archived_title`.

    println!("archived: {archived_title}");
    println!("current: {title}"); // Error: `title` was moved above.
}

The compiler rejects the whole program before it runs. This matters because a use-after-free would otherwise be a runtime memory-safety bug: the old binding could point at storage that another owner already released. Rejecting the code at compile time means every execution of the compiled program follows a valid ownership path, without adding a runtime ownership counter for ordinary String values.

The diagnostic usually points to both sides of the story:

error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `title`
  --> src/main.rs:6:29
   |
3  |     let archived_title = title;
   |                          ----- value moved here
...
6  |     println!("current: {title}");
   |                          ^^^^^ value borrowed here after move

docs.title: Checkpoint 2
docs.text:
What does borrow of moved value: title tell you?

The compiler detected a slow heap allocation while the program was running title was copied twice and needs manual cleanup title was moved earlier, then used again later Check answer

The fix is to choose the intended ownership design. Use the new owner:

println!("current: {archived_title}");

Or make an explicit independent copy when both values must own their data:

let archived_title = title.clone();
println!("current: {title}");
println!("archived: {archived_title}");

clone() is an explicit heap-data copy, so it has a cost and communicates a different design from a cheap move of the String handle.

docs.title: Moving into and out of functions
docs.text:
Passing an owned value to a function uses the same rule. The function becomes the owner for the duration of the call, then drops the value when its parameter leaves scope:

fn take_ownership(text: String) {
    println!("inside function: {text}");
} // `text` is dropped here

let message = String::from("hello");
take_ownership(message);
// `message` cannot be used here because ownership moved into the function.

If the caller needs the value afterward, the function can return ownership:

fn give_back(text: String) -> String {
    text
}

let message = give_back(String::from("hello"));
println!("{message}");

Returning ownership works, but borrowing is often a better fit when a function only needs temporary access. The next lessons build on this distinction.

docs.title: Complete runnable example
docs.text:
The lesson displays the same source file used by the matching demo:

fn take_ownership(text: String) {
    // `text` is the owner inside this function.
    println!("inside function: {text}");
} // `text` leaves scope, so Rust drops the String here.

fn give_back(text: String) -> String {
    // The function receives ownership and returns it to its caller.
    text
}

fn main() {
    let first = String::from("hello");
    let second = first; // Move the String handle and heap allocation to `second`.

    // `first` cannot be used here: it no longer owns the String.
    println!("after move: {second}");

    take_ownership(second); // Move ownership into the function.

    let returned = give_back(String::from("ownership returned"));
    println!("returned: {returned}");
}

Run it from the repository root:

rustc examples/02-ownership-and-borrowing/02-move-semantics/main.rs \
  -o /tmp/rust-move-semantics
/tmp/rust-move-semantics

Expected output:

after move: hello
inside function: hello
returned: ownership returned

docs.title: Exercise: read the compiler message
docs.text:
1. Uncomment println!("{first}"); after let second = first.
  2. Compile the program again.
  3. Find the line that says borrow of moved value or use of moved value.
  4. In the diagnostic, identify the line marked value moved here and the line marked value borrowed here after move.
  5. Restore the working version, then change take_ownership to return the String and assign the returned value back to a variable.

The compiler error is telling you that the ownership story in the code is incomplete: decide whether the function should consume the value, return it, or borrow it.

docs.title: The brief version
docs.text:
Ownership is Rust's rule for deciding which variable is responsible for a value. Every value has one owner. When the owner leaves its scope, Rust cleans up the value automatically.

Borrowing means using a reference to a value without taking ownership. &name creates a shared borrow, so a function can read a value while the caller keeps owning it. Rust checks that references never outlive the value they refer to.

flowchart LR
  O[Owner] -->|borrows with &| R[Reference]
  R -->|reads temporarily| V[Value]
  O -->|still owns| V

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
fn count_letters(text: &String) -> usize {
    text.len()
}

fn main() {
    let message = String::from("Rust");
    println!("{} has {} letters", message, count_letters(&message));
    println!("The owner can still use: {message}");
}

The function borrows message, so ownership stays in main. Compile and run the complete example from the repository root:

rustc examples/02-ownership-and-borrowing/main.rs -o /tmp/rust-ownership
/tmp/rust-ownership

Expected output:

Rust has 4 letters
The owner can still use: Rust
